summary: Defines the ChaCha20 stream cipher and the Poly1305 authenticator, both on their own and combined as an authenticated encryption (AEAD) algorithm. It replaces RFC 7539, which was a stable reference and implementation guide from the Crypto Forum Research Group.

eli5.summary: ChaCha20 scrambles a message so only the right person can read it, and Poly1305 adds a seal that shows nobody tampered with it. Together they do both jobs at once.

questions: why use chacha20 instead of aes
subtitle: A fast software cipher and a one-time authenticator, defined stand-alone and combined into one AEAD for IETF protocols.

tldr.problem: AES is the practical choice almost everywhere, but it is slow on platforms without AES hardware, many implementations are open to cache-collision timing attacks, and there is no fast fallback if AES is ever weakened.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the ChaCha20 stream cipher, the Poly1305 one-time authenticator, and AEAD_CHACHA20_POLY1305, which uses ChaCha20 to encrypt and to derive a Poly1305 key that tags the result.
tldr.outcome: Protocols get a stable, well-specified encryption-plus-integrity primitive with test vectors. It replaces RFC 7539 and merges its errata.

today: RFC 8439 obsoletes RFC 7539, merging the errata filed against it and adding a little text to the Security Considerations. It is an Informational RFC from the IRTF's Crypto Forum Research Group, and the unit metadata lists nothing that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Second Cipher
sections.content:
AES is the gold standard in encryption, and on most modern platforms it is four to ten times as fast as 3DES. The RFC sees three problems with that. If cryptanalysis ever found a weakness in AES, the only other widely supported cipher, 3DES, would be much slower. AES is also considerably slower on platforms without dedicated hardware, and many AES implementations are vulnerable to cache-collision timing attacks.

The document defines three algorithms: the ChaCha20 cipher, the Poly1305 authenticator, and the AEAD_CHACHA20_POLY1305 combination. None is new here. They were defined in papers by D. J. Bernstein, and the RFC's job is to be a stable reference and implementation guide for IETF documents. ChaCha20 is described as around three times as fast as AES on platforms that lack specialized AES hardware.
sections.eli5: If everyone locks their doors with the same kind of lock and someone finds a way to pick it, everyone is in trouble. This gives people a second, different lock that is also quick to use.

sections.title: The ChaCha20 Stream Cipher
sections.content:
ChaCha20 works on a state of sixteen 32-bit words. The first four words are fixed constants, the next eight hold the 256-bit key, word 12 is a block counter, and words 13 to 15 hold a 96-bit nonce. The basic step is the quarter round, which mixes four words using only addition modulo 2^32, XOR and fixed left rolls (by 16, 12, 8 and 7 bits).

The block function runs 20 rounds, alternating column rounds and diagonal rounds, with eight quarter rounds per pair. It then adds the original input words to the result and serializes it as 64 bytes of random-looking output. To encrypt, ChaCha20 calls the block function with increasing counter values and XORs the resulting keystream with the plaintext. Extra keystream in the last block is discarded. Decryption is the same operation applied to the ciphertext.

The original ChaCha had a 64-bit nonce and a 64-bit block count. This RFC uses a 96-bit nonce and a 32-bit counter to match the recommendations of RFC 5116, which limits one key and nonce combination to 2^32 blocks, or 256 GB.
sections.eli5: ChaCha20 is a machine that turns a secret key into an endless stream of scribble. You mix the scribble into your message to hide it, and mix the same scribble in again to get it back.

sections.title: The Poly1305 Authenticator
sections.content:
Poly1305 is a one-time authenticator. It takes a 32-byte one-time key and a message and produces a 16-byte tag. The key is split into two halves, r and s. The value r is first clamped, which means clearing certain bits so that it has the required form.

The message is cut into 16-byte blocks. For each block, the algorithm adds a one bit beyond the block's length, adds the number to an accumulator, multiplies by r and reduces modulo the prime 2^130-5. At the end s is added and the low 128 bits are written out as the tag.

The key pair must be unpredictable and must not be reused. Section 2.6 therefore defines how to derive it from ChaCha20: run the block function with the 256-bit session key, block counter zero and the nonce, and use the first 256 bits of the output. The first 128 bits are clamped to form r and the next 128 bits become s. The nonce for this MUST be unique per invocation, so it MUST NOT be randomly generated.
sections.eli5: Poly1305 stamps a short secret seal on a message. Change even one letter and the seal no longer matches. Each seal is made from a fresh secret so no one can reuse it.

sections.title: The AEAD Construction
sections.content:
AEAD_CHACHA20_POLY1305 takes a 256-bit key, a 96-bit nonce that differs for every invocation with the same key, a plaintext of any length, and optional additional authenticated data (AAD). Three steps produce the output:

  • Generate a Poly1305 one-time key from the key and nonce, as in Section 2.6.
  • Encrypt the plaintext with ChaCha20, using the same key and nonce and an initial counter of 1.
  • Run Poly1305 over the AAD, zero padding to a multiple of 16 bytes, the ciphertext, more padding, and then the AAD length and ciphertext length, each as a 64-bit little-endian integer.

The output is the ciphertext, which is the same length as the plaintext, followed by a 128-bit tag. To decrypt, the receiver recomputes the tag over the AAD and the ciphertext (not the plaintext), compares it with the received tag, and accepts the message only if they match. A single invocation can protect at most 2^32-1 blocks of 64 bytes, which the RFC notes should be enough for traffic protocols such as IPsec and TLS but may be too small for file or disk encryption.

Section 2.7 also records a deliberate omission: Poly1305 is biased and cannot be reused with the same key, so it is not suitable as a pseudorandom function, and the document does not specify one.
sections.eli5: First you scramble the message, then you stamp a seal over the scrambled message and the label on the outside of the envelope. The reader checks the seal first, and only opens the envelope if it matches.

sections.title: Implementation Advice
sections.content:
The RFC offers two practical tips. For ChaCha20, copy the state and do the rounds on the copy, so the next block only needs the block counter incremented. This saves approximately 5.5% of the cycles.

For Poly1305, it is not recommended to use a generic big number library such as the one in OpenSSL, because such libraries allocate memory dynamically, which costs performance and side-channel security. The RFC points to constant-time implementations in NaCl and in poly1305-donna, and notes that a naive constant-time approach using 288-bit integers is possible.
sections.eli5: It is quicker to keep a spare copy of your starting numbers than to rebuild them each time. And for the sealing step, use tools made for the job rather than a giant general-purpose calculator.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
ChaCha20 is designed to provide 256-bit security. Poly1305 is designed so that forged messages are rejected with a probability of 1-(n/(2^102)) for a 16n-byte message, even after 2^64 legitimate messages. The RFC leaves the proofs to the cited academic papers.

The most important rule is nonce uniqueness. Counters and LFSRs are acceptable ways to generate nonces. If a nonce repeats, both the Poly1305 key and the keystream repeat, which reveals the XOR of the plaintexts.

Implementations MUST compare tags with a constant-time function rather than something like C's memcmp(), and any protocol using this algorithm MUST include the complete tag. Tag truncation MUST NOT be done.

The algorithms use only additions, XORs and fixed rolls, so they can be written to run in constant time without key-dependent memory access, which avoids timing leaks through cache misses. Poly1305 arithmetic needs care, because a naive implementation with a generic big number library will not be constant time.
sections.eli5: Never use the same one-time code twice, or a snoop can learn secrets by comparing your two messages. And check the seal in a way that takes the same time every time, so nobody can guess it from how fast you say no.
